newsitem.title: ITALY: FORECAST - Italy to cut interest rates by March.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Italy to cut interest rates by March.

text.p: A long-awaited reduction in Italy's key interest rates will come at the latest by end-March, but probable changes in the global rate scenario could make any further easing tougher, economists said.

A Reuter quarterly poll of 16 analysts showed forecasts were for a 75 basis point cut in the Bank of Italy's 7.50 discount rate in the first quarter, followed by a further fall to 6.25 percent by the end of 1997.

"The timing and size of the first cut are dependent on metalworkers and employers reaching an accord on renewing a pay contract for 1996-98," said Pompeo Pontone, bond market analyst at Credito Italiano.

Analysts said Bank of Italy governor Antonio Fazio made this clear on January 13 when he said that while great progress had been made in bringing inflation down, "there are risks coming from public finance and labour costs, and monetary policy has to reflect this."

"The central bank could even cut the discount rate by one percentage point if the long-running dispute in the metal and engineering sector is resolved with a non-inflationary pay rise," Pontone added.

Gianluca Sanna, economist at Banco di Sardegna, saw a 50-75 bp cut this month if preliminary January consumer price inflation data from 11 sample Italian cities due on Monday and Tuesday are positive.
An improvement in state finances and continuing benign inflation figures could set the scene for a second rate cut.
"But from the start of the second half this year the scenario abroad will become less favourable, showing more sustained growth in Germany and the United States," Sanna said.

Marcello Pericoli, economist at San Paolo Bank in London, agreed. "Italy and Spain will struggle to keep up, it will be difficult for them to oppose a trend of rising interest rates and bond spreads will tend to widen out," he said.
The bullish phase on Italian debt markets in recent weeks has seen the spread between 10-year Italian Btps and Bunds narrow to a historic low of 150 basis points.

Over the coming months analysts expect to see a point of equilibrium around 155/160 bps and forecast a widening out towards 170 at the end of the year. Some non-Italian forecasters were more pessimistic, seeing 200/230 bps at year-end.

On rates, the U.S. Federal Reserve will get the ball rolling with a hike of some 25 basis points at the beginning of the summer, according to Pontone. "But this will be more of a fine-tuning move than a reversal of monetary policy," he said.
"The Bundesbank will be next and could revise upwards its end-year repo rate," San Paolo's Pericoli said.
"In this way Italy and Spain will be pushed further away from the European economic and monetary union (EMU) deadline, but this won't be too dramatic," he added.

"Italy will be able to negotiate EMU entry with its European partners after January 1, 1999. A clear accord and a goal which is just put off a bit will protect the markets from the risk of a violent sell-off," Credito Italiano noted.

The scenario for three-month Treasury bill (BOT) yields, and for 10-year fixed-rate bonds (BTP) at the other end of the curve, will reflect expectations of interest rate moves, the analysts' forecasts showed.
